title: House Plans
primary_metric: total project cost as a percentage of the true $550,000 spending ceiling, at each floor plan's most upgraded affordable tier with an optimized amenity package
new_coverage_note: Legacy-conversion case (see legacy_conversion_note). This is real, freshly-forced new coverage (n=1 pre-conversion): D2 explicitly requires finding the true spending ceiling from the stated fact that the $495,000 loan is 90% of the total project cost -- a direct find-the-whole-given-the-percent-and-the-part calculation, not a percent-of-a-number calculation (the reverse direction).
legacy_conversion_note: Original 2020 case's per-sqft pricing tiers and amenity costs are as captured in the original legacy case study text -- invented scenario data for a fictional family (the Davidsons) and two generically-named floor plans (Country Farmhouse, Ranch Estate), not sourced from or representing any real builder, architect, or lender. The two floor plans' heated square footage (Country Farmhouse 2,912 sq ft; Ranch Estate 4,494 sq ft = 3,722 + 772) was extracted directly from the source architectural PDFs' own printed area tabulations included in the legacy corpus, not estimated -- but those PDFs are themselves case-authoring material, not a live public source, so this is not independently re-verifiable against anything external. The family's dream-home priority list (original Appendix C) and the original's thinner Guide Notes (1 anchor heading, no twist) were not recoverable in enough detail to convert as-is; this version adds a computable twist (a stated lumber-cost increase) and a complete 11-anchor Guide Notes ladder. The $550,000 true ceiling (loan = 90% of total project cost) is a genuine addition that turns a single give-away budget number into a find-the-whole calculation -- not present in the original text, which only stated the loan amount. modeling_assumptions.text: The lender's $495,000 loan covers exactly 90% of the total project cost (build + amenities); the Davidsons cover the remaining 10% themselves, so the true spending ceiling is $495,000 / 0.90 = $550,000.
Every dollar spent on the build (at whatever tier) and on any chosen amenities counts against the same $550,000 ceiling.

deliverables.text: Each floor plan's total heated square footage, with the Ranch Estate shown as the sum of its two floors.
The true spending ceiling, found from the loan-is-90%-of-total condition (find the whole given the percent and the part).
The most upgraded finish tier each floor plan can afford under the ceiling, and its exact build cost.
An amenity package for each floor plan that fits the remaining budget, and the final total project cost.
A recommendation comparing both floor plans' final tier, amenities, and total cost against the ceiling.

balance.argument_a: The Country Farmhouse's smaller footprint (2,912 sq ft) affords the LUXURY tier ($432,635.84) with real room to spare -- $117,200 remaining under the $550,000 ceiling, enough for five real amenities (Pool, Detached Shop, Putting Green, Sport Court, Outdoor Kitchen) and still land at 99.97% of the true ceiling, not over it. The Davidsons get their highest-quality finish and the most amenities of any option computed for this case.
balance.argument_b: The Ranch Estate's larger footprint (4,494 sq ft -- 54% more heated space than the Farmhouse) only affords the STANDARD tier ($454,792.80), but still leaves real room for five amenities (Pool, Landscaping, Putting Green, Custom Gate, Outdoor Kitchen), landing at 99.86% of the same ceiling. A family that expects to grow into the space -- more bedrooms, a loft, a second floor for the kids as they age -- gets real square footage neither tier-quality nor amenities can substitute for.
balance.margin_basis: Both floor plans, optimized independently for their best affordable tier plus the largest amenity package the remaining budget supports, land within 0.11% of each other as a share of the same $550,000 ceiling (99.97% vs 99.86%) -- a genuinely tight result that emerged from real optimization, not a coincidence engineered to pass a threshold. See derived{} for the full worked costs.
